item.content:encoded:
Point of note: is "100 to 160 grams" (grammes?) the entire mass of all 79 pieces, or per piece?

A 2-gramme piece of chocolate is pretty small. But a ~130 gramme one would be huge. A typical medium size block is 100g. I think a Malteser might only be 2g, but then those are mostly heavily aerated honeycomb and not very much chocolate wrapped around.

Also, why is the measurement so vague? Does it continually vary somehow? Does the chocolate regenerate, at a higher rate as the amount left falls, until you reach a point at 100g where it regenerates faster than you can reasonably remove it (or you approach a point where the pile of removed chocolate switches to being the collection that gains mass / both of them start doing it), and conversely it stops on reaching 160g (…per pile)?

item.title: Re: Staff Post - Open
item.content:encoded:
That's because it's the nominal lower bound for a typical refrigerator's temperature range (go below about 3 to 4 celcius and you risk evaporative frosting effects). The actual acceptable range, which may well be experienced in a fridge with a somewhat slack thermostat (averaging about 6'C) is generally taken as 4 to 8 celcius.

In which case saying to keep it at or below 7 celcius would suggest either a fridge set just a little colder than normal, or it could be an economy measure; with a stat set to that you might see an upper temperature around 9 to 11 celcius, which still gives us an acceptable safety margin below 15 celcius in case of power outages, fridge failure, or the actual lowest possible melting point being lower than all those yet observed, without spending quite as much on cooling as with normal mass cold storage. Which could be significant for budgetary purposes if the chocolate is being kept in a cold lockbox (or just one of those electrically chilled picnic boxes) all to itself to minimise the risk of cross contamination.

I like this because it takes place near where I live and makes people sound delicious however there where a few things that bug me. Now when you say the agents were "embeded" in the police force, it makes me think this was a long term assignment which is a little odd to me. why would the foundation waste resources on keeping agents in the police force when they could easily monitor police reports through hacking the database and monitor police radios? And how would these 2 agents have realized it was the chocolates that was the cause of the cannibalism? Does the chocolate have a specific chemical makeup and was identified in all the victims stomachs during autopsy or did the agents actually witness the chocolate in motion? It would be cool if the discovery of said chocolates was a little more specific.in my head it played out like-
(Agent1 and 2 enter bakery)
Agent1- yo Dawg what you think did this?
(Agent 2 opens fridge)
Agent 2- ayy nigga these chocolates look sneaky as f***
Agent 1- yo pocket that shit bro we outtie yolo/swag!

But I'm probably just being a little nitpicky. Like I said I like the story ;D
